gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured figure for any laptop screen extender. The one lab test I found of a FOPO triple extender is Notebookcheck's: the 12-inch model measured 193.1 cd/m² maximum brightness, 247:1 contrast and 79% sRGB. The Gadgeteer's hands-on test of FOPO's 15-inch triple, which FOPO rates for 15–17-inch laptops, ran it on an 18-inch Asus G18. Only one of that laptop's USB-C ports carried video, so one side screen had to use HDMI plus a separate USB-C power cable.
standout_why: Compared against WorkCocoon's 17-inch extender page (result 1 in both chats) and Cevaton's 17-inch compatibility page (result 9). WorkCocoon says it assessed listed specs and never says it tested a unit. Its only figure is Arzopa's own 103% sRGB claim, and it gives no measured brightness, weight or power. Cevaton gives only screen sizes, resolutions and ports, with no measurements. It is also the maker's own blog. GradedPicks would not open because of a certificate error, so I could not compare against it. None of the rival pages I read has a named reviewer's measurement or a test on a laptop of 17 inches or larger.
decides: This confirms the pick rather than changing it. In the only named hands-on test on a laptop of 17 inches or larger, what decided the setup was how many USB-C ports carry video, not the screens. A large gaming laptop may have only one, so the second added screen needs HDMI plus separate power, or a driver. That supports putting each row's video path first on the page. Notebookcheck's numbers, taken on FOPO's 12-inch triple and not on a 16-inch FOPO we link, also show FOPO's extender panels can test well below the 250–300 nits they are sold at. The page can't claim our FOPO rows match a 17-inch laptop's own screen, because no reviewer has measured the S788, S10, S11 or S9G. No measured figure I found picks a winner among the candidates.
